title: Sliding Window Pattern Explained: A LeetCode Guide (2026)
description: The sliding window pattern explained: fixed versus dynamic windows, why it is O(n), the maximising trap, and the five problems that teach the whole pattern.
content:
The nested loop that quietly times out

The problem asks for the longest substring without repeating characters. You write the obvious thing: for every starting index, extend to the right until you hit a duplicate, track the best length. It passes the example. It passes the second example. Then the hidden test arrives with a 100,000-character string and the submission dies.

Nothing in your code is wrong. It is just doing the same work over and over. The sliding window pattern is the fix, and it turns a large family of O(n²) solutions into O(n) with a change of perspective rather than a clever trick.

The analogy: reading through a mail slot

Picture a long strip of paper covered in letters, and a card with a rectangular slot cut into it. You lay the card over the strip and can only see the letters inside the slot.

To examine the whole strip, you do not lift the card and lay it down again at every position — that is the nested loop. You slide it. When the right edge moves one letter forward, exactly one letter enters the slot. When the left edge moves forward, exactly one leaves. Everything in between stays where it was and does not need re-reading.

That is the entire idea. The window carries its own running state, and each step updates that state by one addition and at most one removal instead of recomputing it from scratch.

When to reach for it

The recognition signal is specific, which makes this one of the easiest patterns to spot:

  • The answer is a contiguous subarray or substring — not a subsequence, not a subset.
  • The question asks for a longest, shortest, maximum or minimum under some constraint.
  • The state you track is cheap to update incrementally: a running sum, a count of characters, a set of what is currently inside.

If the elements do not have to be adjacent, this is not a sliding window — that is usually dynamic programming or a heap. If the array is sorted and you want a pair summing to a target, that is two pointers, which is a close cousin but moves both ends toward each other rather than dragging a window rightward.

Fixed window or dynamic window?

Every sliding window problem is one of two shapes, and deciding which one you are looking at is the whole battle.

Fixed window

The problem gives you the window size. "Maximum average subarray of size K." Both edges move together, in lockstep, one step at a time. There is no decision to make.

The template: build the first K elements, record the result, then for every subsequent index add the entering element, subtract the leaving element, record again. One pass, constant extra state.

Dynamic window

The size is not given — it is what you are solving for. "Smallest subarray with a sum of at least target." "Longest substring with at most K distinct characters."

Here the two edges move independently, and the shape is always the same:

  1. Expand: move the right edge forward one element and add it to your running state.
  2. Check: is the window still valid under the constraint?
  3. Shrink: while it is invalid, move the left edge forward, removing elements from the state, until it is valid again.
  4. Record: after each step, update your best answer.

The reason this is O(n) rather than O(n²) is worth stating out loud in an interview, because it is the part interviewers probe. Each of the two pointers only ever moves forward, and neither can move more than n times. So even though there is a loop inside a loop, the total number of pointer movements across the whole run is at most 2n.

The detail that decides the problem

There is one question that determines the correct template, and getting it wrong is the most common bug in this pattern: are you maximising or minimising?

When you want the smallest valid window, record the answer while shrinking — every time the window is valid, it might be the new minimum, and you keep shrinking to see if a smaller one also works.

When you want the largest valid window, record the answer after restoring validity, and you often do not need a shrinking loop at all — a single step is enough, because a window that is already at its best-known size never needs to get smaller. This is the subtlety behind Longest Repeating Character Replacement, where a single if replaces the usual while, and where a deliberately stale maximum-frequency count is still correct because you only ever care about the largest window seen.

If you can explain that last point clearly, you are demonstrating exactly the kind of reasoning that separates a memorised solution from an understood one.

Want to master this with video lessons and real case studies? This topic is covered in depth in my Udemy course System Design Fundamentals for Interviews — 5.5 hours, rated 4.8★, built from real interview questions.

The five problems that teach the whole pattern

You do not need twenty of these. Five, in this order, cover every variation you are likely to be asked:

  1. Maximum Average Subarray I — the fixed window in its purest form. Ten minutes.
  2. Minimum Size Subarray Sum — your first dynamic window, minimising. Teaches recording the answer during the shrink.
  3. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters — dynamic window, maximising, with a hash map holding the window contents. The single most-asked problem in this family.
  4. Longest Repeating Character Replacement — the maximising subtlety above, plus a frequency array. This is the one that teaches you the pattern rather than a solution.
  5. Minimum Window Substring — the hard one. Two hash maps and a "how many required characters are currently satisfied" counter. If you can write this from memory, the pattern is yours.

Solve each one, then close the editor and rewrite the template from a blank page. The rewrite is where the learning happens.

Where candidates lose points

  • Shrinking with if when the problem needs while. Minimising problems must keep shrinking as long as the window is valid.
  • Forgetting to remove state on the way out. When the left edge advances, the counter for that element has to be decremented — and removed from the map entirely when it hits zero, or your "distinct count" is wrong.
  • Recording the answer in the wrong place. Inside the shrink loop for minimising, outside it for maximising.
  • Applying it to non-contiguous problems. If the answer allows skipping elements, this pattern cannot express it.

How to talk about this in an interview

A thirty-second answer you can adapt to any window problem:

"The brute force checks every substring, which is O(n²) and will time out at these constraints. But neighbouring substrings overlap almost entirely, so I am recomputing the same counts repeatedly. Instead I will keep a window with two pointers and a running count of what is inside it. I expand the right edge, and while the window violates the constraint I shrink from the left, updating the count as elements enter and leave. Each pointer only moves forward, so the total work is O(n) time and O(k) space, where k is the size of the character set."

Say that before you write a line of code and you have already shown the brute force, the reason it fails, the pattern, the invariant and the complexity.

Key Takeaways

  • Sliding window applies when the answer is a contiguous run and the question asks for a longest, shortest, maximum or minimum under a constraint.
  • Fixed windows move both edges together; dynamic windows expand right and shrink left independently.
  • It is O(n) because each pointer only moves forward — say that out loud, because it is what gets probed.
  • Minimising records the answer while shrinking; maximising records it after validity is restored.
  • Five problems, ending with Minimum Window Substring, cover the entire pattern.

Next Steps

Two pointers is the natural companion and is covered next — same idea of moving indices instead of nesting loops, but converging from both ends rather than dragging a window. If you have not chosen a study order yet, start from the 15 LeetCode patterns guide, which ranks them by payoff. Preparing for a specific loop?
